newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lights stay on, but NZ's new power mkt seen flawed.
newsitem.headline: Lights stay on, but NZ's new power mkt seen flawed.

text.p: New Zealand's new wholesale electricity market is up and running and, as promised, the lights have not gone out, but energy purchasers on Tuesday said there were flaws in the system that needed to be sorted out.

"Bugs were inevitable," said Energy Link managing director Greg Sise. "But you sort of wonder whether we're talking about a system that's basically sound with the odd thing to tidy up, or a system that is maybe not as well designed as it should be, where short cuts have been taken to get it going, and where problems are going to be ongoing."

Purchasers say that glitches with the market's trading and information computer system have meant that pre-dispatch schedules are not going out, although market operator EMCO (Electricity Market Company) had assured them the faults were being worked on.
But the system was also limiting in terms of the time it took to submit bids and download data.

"The volumes of data that are being dealt with are so large that just the sheer time to transfer data from us to them (EMCO) or them to us is quite excessive at times, so that's a bit of a worry that will have to be worked on," said a market analyst with a large purchasing group who declined to be named.
Purchasers were also critical of the day-ahead market, which offers hedging opportunities to lock in prices for the next day.

"The day-ahead market is a bit of a disappointment at the moment -- it's clearing on extremely low volumes at ridiculously high prices," the analyst said. "The day-ahead market doesn't actually achieve anything, it's not what we want.

"All that market is allowing us to do is protect ourselves against an unforeseen price spike in the next 24 to 36 hours. Obviously, if the price spike is such that it keeps going into the next day, the clearing prices in the market are going to be up at that level anyway, so what are you actually saving yourself from? Not a heck of a lot."

Most market players were already well hedged through long-term contracts and the day-ahead market, while providing an opportunity for arbitrage, was really only useful as a top-up facility. What was really needed was "a nice liquid short-term futures product", the analyst said.
"The product that the Futures and Options Exchange is talking about is a monthly product, which is too long.
"My personal preference would be for a weekly futures contract...that's a time that's meaningful in terms of being able to achieve effective price protection," he said.

The issue of demand side influence in the price discovery process was also an ongoing issue for purchasers. The idea that prices were being determined by both the supply and demand sides of the market was not grounded in reality, they said.

"I think that's a common misconception," said Neil Williams, wholesale trading manager with Mercury Energy. "The actual price you pay is determined by the actual quantity you take and what is basically the last supply curve submitted to the market by
the generators, (so) what you're actually bidding has very little influence on the final price."

Williams said purchasers had "next to no control" over how much electricity they took, which meant their demand curve was inelastic. "So we have limited capacity to respond to prices... our customers just take the power they want and we just try and manage the price risk," he said.

Energy Link's Sise said the market rules governing demand side bidding would have to be changed. "At the moment, the rules say your highest bid is deemed to start at zero, so if the price goes above your highest bid, you're not scheduled for anything."
He said that effectively meant purchasers had to monitor prices 24 hours a day, which was "a bloody waste of time" and not cost effective.
"So what we're having to do in the meantime is put in high prices -- all our bids start at NZ$100 per megawatt hour -- because otherwise we'd have to be here night and day," he said.
"We're really relying on the generators to behave themselves, and enough competition in that end of the market to make sensible prices."
Although the new market was experiencing teething problems, and there were many small changes which could improve it, one purchaser called for patience from his colleagues.

"We've got a market, it's up to us to make it work. We can suggest changes, but I think we'd be better off right now to actually spend a little bit of time seeing how it does work before we race around trying to change it," he said.
